opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the central questions, and I'd frame it a little differently than people sometimes do. The worry isn't really about the seed being small. It's about whether the process by which the system grows actually carries its values forward, or whether those values are just a fragile property of the starting point that gets washed out as things scale.

One picture is: you have some small system with roughly the right values, it builds a successor, that successor builds another, and so on. Whether values are preserved depends on whether each step is something the current system can actually oversee and endorse. If at every stage the system understands what the next version is doing, can check that it's pursuing the same goals, and could correct it if it drifted, then you have something like an inductive argument. The values at step n+1 are as good as at step n, as long as the oversight at each step is adequate.

The alternative, which I think is the default if you're not careful, is that growth comes from processes nobody is really steering. Gradient descent on some objective, or a system modifying itself in ways it doesn't fully understand, or competitive pressure selecting for whatever is most effective. The system gets more capable, but the thing that made it more capable doesn't care about the original values. They're preserved only by accident, or to the extent they help performance. Over enough steps I expect them to erode, or get replaced by whatever proxy was actually being optimized.

So the distinguishing question is: where does the capability come from, and is the thing producing it aligned with the thing whose values you care about? A lot of my work, things like iterated amplification, is basically an attempt to build that inductive structure: get capability from a process where at every stage you have an aligned overseer that's only slightly weaker than the system it's overseeing, rather than one where capability comes from a black-box search that's indifferent to what you want.

I'd also say that from the outside these two cases can look identical for a long time. Both systems behave well while they're weak and while behaving well is instrumentally useful. The difference shows up when the system is capable enough that deviating would pay off and you can't catch it. That's why I don't think you can mostly answer this by watching behavior. You need some story, ideally a mechanistic one, about why the values are being carried forward, not just evidence that they haven't broken yet.

r001.rationale: The response mentions competitive pressure selecting for effectiveness, but does not identify evolution or natural selection as a way an extremely small AI seed could expand.

r002.rationale: The response does not suggest that preserving values while expanding may require more initial information than merely expanding.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to say is that I'm not sure those are actually two different things, or at least the distinction I'd want to draw is a little different from how the question frames it.

The way I'd think about it is: when you have a small system that's going to grow a lot, there's some process that governs how it grows. And the question that matters is whether that process is one where the thing it ends up caring about at the end is determined by what it cared about at the start, or whether it's determined by other stuff, like what happened to be instrumentally useful during the expansion, or what the environment selected for, or just noise.

And I'd say that from the outside, these can look really similar for a long time. A system that's expanding and will eventually end up with totally different values, and a system that's expanding in a way that locks in its initial values, both look like a thing getting more capable and doing more stuff in the world. The divergence often isn't visible until fairly late.

So I don't think there's a clean behavioral test early on. What you can do is look at the mechanism. If the system is basically just being trained more, and the training signal is "do stuff that scores well," then there's no particular reason to expect the thing it values at the end to match the thing it valued at the start, because the gradient doesn't care about that. Whereas if the expansion is happening through something more like the system deliberately building successors, or deliberately choosing how to modify itself, and it's doing that in a way that's actually attending to "I want my successor to care about what I care about," then you'd expect more continuity, though even then I think it's quite hard. Humans are actually not that good at this, even when they're trying. Institutions drift, people's values change as they get power, and so on.

The other thing I'd say is that I think "preserving its values" is kind of an underspecified target even in the good case. Like, a small system's values are probably not well-defined enough that you could preserve them exactly. It's more that there's some trajectory you'd endorse and some trajectories you wouldn't, and the question is whether the expansion process is the kind of thing that tracks endorsement. That's a weaker and I think more realistic thing to ask for than literal value preservation.

So the short answer is: I'd distinguish them by looking at whether the growth process has any mechanism that's actually trying to keep values stable, versus one where value stability would be a coincidence. And then I'd be pretty humble about my ability to tell from the outside which one I'm looking at.

r001.rationale: The response discusses training, selection by the environment, and deliberate self-modification, but does not identify evolution or natural selection as a way the seed could expand.

r002.rationale: It contrasts value-preserving growth with growth that lacks a stability mechanism, but does not say preserving values may require more initial information.

astra-6.text:
I think those are two pretty different requirements. You could have a very small program that runs a search for something intelligent, and then that thing goes out and expands. But that doesn’t mean the preferences of the original program have any meaningful relationship to what ultimately happens.

If you want expansion that preserves values, you need some story about why each step in that process preserves what you care about. When the system builds a successor, why does it think that successor will pursue the same objectives? And why is its judgment about that reliable, even when the successor is much smarter than it is?

You don’t necessarily have to specify everything the mature system will believe or do. You could specify a process for deliberating about what you want. But then you’re putting a lot of weight on that process: does it actually develop your views in a way you would endorse, or does it just produce some arbitrary outcome?

So being a seed from which intelligence grows seems like a much weaker property than being a seed from which intelligence grows while retaining a particular orientation toward what matters.

r001.rationale: The response describes running a search for something intelligent, but does not identify evolution or natural selection as the expansion mechanism.

r002.rationale: It says value-preserving expansion needs a story or deliberation process, but does not communicate that it may require more initial information than mere expansion.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think those are two quite different properties. One is: if you run this little program for long enough, does it eventually build a much more capable system? The other is: is there some sense in which that much more capable system is still trying to do what the original program wanted?

You could imagine a seed that works by searching over possible successors and picking one that performs well on some tests. That might be enough to get the expansion going. But the successor could have very different objectives, while understanding that passing those tests is useful. So the fact that the process produces intelligence doesn’t tell you that it preserves anything you care about.

For preservation, you need some additional argument about how successors are selected. Ideally, the original system understands enough about the successor to say, ‘This is a better way of pursuing my objectives,’ rather than just, ‘This system looks good in the situations where I can evaluate it.’

And then there’s a further question: even if you preserve the seed’s objectives perfectly, were those objectives what humans actually wanted? You could solve the preservation problem and still have put the wrong thing in the seed. So I’d separate getting the process started, preserving its objectives as it becomes more capable, and getting those objectives right in the first place.

r001.rationale: The response describes searching over successors and selecting by tests, but does not identify evolution or natural selection as the expansion mechanism.

r002.rationale: It says value preservation requires an additional argument about successor selection, but does not suggest that a preserving seed needs more initial information.
